text: The 'price of admission' pitch: traverse rightward across gravelly, gently down-sloping class-2 ledges from the notch's east side, then a steep crack, a V-groove and a finger traverse lead to a small tree anchor — unglamorous but necessary to reach the better rock above.
runs: a steep crack a v groove and a finger traverse

text: The most direct line up Inspiration Peak: about 600 ft (4 pitches) of clean rock, reached by crossing the glacier to a small buttress under the south face. Climb up and right to a right-trending ramp, belay below a corner system, then trend up and left to connect with the obvious 'Great Gash' — a chimney splitting the upper south face — and chimney to the top. First climbed by Mike Heath and Bill Sumner on June 18, probably in 1969.
runs: a right trending ramp belay below a corner system

text: Access a small buttress under the south face via the glacier, then climb up and right (low 5th class, ~5.7) to a right-trending ramp system. Follow the ramp for several pitches until it forks, then work up and left to the obvious deep, jagged gash splitting the upper south face. Climb the gash via a mix of face and chimney climbing (5.8 max) to a chockstone just below the easy summit pitch. Excellent, continuous rock throughout; named among Fred Beckey's 100 favorite North American climbs.
runs: access a small buttress under the south face via the glacier
a chockstone just below the easy summit pitch

text: The gash is the namesake feature — solid face and chimney climbing on mostly good rock once you're in it.
runs: solid face and chimney climbing on mostly good rock

text: The South Face climbs a solid red-rock ramp on Red Mountain's south side via several class 3 pitches, typically done unroped given moderate exposure; most parties finish left onto the class 2 scrambling route on the west side of the south ridge. Climbers wanting more technical terrain can continue directly up the steep summit block at class 4/low 5th class, which requires a rope for the exposure. This is the most solid rock found on the peak (large slabs), in contrast to the notoriously loose rock elsewhere on Red Mountain.
runs: on the west side of the south ridge
the most solid rock found on the peak

text: Ascends the broad, comparatively solid south-facing ramp/slabs of the mountain via several easy, enjoyable class-3 pitches; most parties climb it unroped. Near the top the direct summit block steepens to class 4 or low 5th and becomes 'roofy' overhead — most parties instead traverse left onto the class-2 hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge rather than continue straight up.
runs: hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge

text: Standard descent follows the class 2 scrambling line on the west side of the south ridge back down. If the party continued up the steep summit block direct, a rappel using tree anchors with webbing and rap rings is an option.
runs: on the west side of the south ridge

text:
The rock is the marker and it is bright red. You are looking for a low-angle gully or ramp of solid, bright red rock at the base of the mountain — solid is the operative word, because it is the most solid rock on a peak otherwise famous for being fractured. The colour and the low angle together identify it; nothing else on this flank looks like it.

And the overshoot test is the one to remember, because it works without seeing anything: if you reach Red Mountain Pond, you have gone too far. Popping out of the trees on the flank of Red commonly puts a party too far west; the pond tells you so unambiguously. Turn back east and traverse on heather until the red gully appears.

What the first ground should feel like: class 3, no gear required, two pitches of it. If you are pulling on anything hard from the ground you are not in the ramp.

Where it leads, so you can check yourself later: you pop over a small ridge into the main gully below the summit. Keep going up that until the summit block above you turns steep and roofy. That roofy steepening is the signal to move left onto the class 2 hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge — or, if you want it, to continue directly up the block at class 4 or low 5 with a rope.
runs: hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge

text: The original 1941 line up Lundin's south face, rising from the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek. Several low-5th-class pitches lead to a slab; the final pitch above it is steeper before topping out near the true (westernmost) summit.
runs: from the headwaters of commonwealth creek several low 5th
pitches lead to a slab the final pitch

text: Climb the South Face of Lundin, which rises from the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek. Several low-5th pitches lead to a slab; the final pitch after this is steeper.
runs: rises from the headwaters of commonwealth creek several low 5th pitches lead to a slab the final pitch after this is steeper

text: Approach as for the West Ridge into Commonwealth/Lundin Basin, then rope up at the base of the south face. Several low-5th pitches lead to a slab, with a steeper final pitch to fin…
runs: several low 5th pitches lead to a slab

text: Approach as for the West Ridge into Commonwealth/Lundin Basin, then rope up at the base of the south face. Several low-5th pitches lead to a slab, with a steeper final pitch to finish. Descend via the Southeast Ridge back into the basin.
runs: several low 5th pitches lead to a slab

text: Follows the obvious crack in the middle of the south face wall starting from the notch: climb through a bulge, then trend left through two right-facing corners to a tree just below the summit block. At 220 feet, the whole route goes in one pitch with a 70m rope (or can be broken into two with a 60m rope). The route wanders, so expect to place extra alpine draws to manage rope drag; some loose blocks and flakes are present and the rock carries lichen from relatively light traffic.
runs: the obvious crack in the middle of the

text: 2 single-rope raps from the south side of the summit
runs: single rope raps from the south side of the summit

text: From the notch, climb the obvious crack in the middle of the south face through a bulge.
runs: the obvious crack in the middle of the

text: MP source explicitly states 'bring about a 1.5 rack [tips to #3 cams], add more depending on confidence' and 'lots of alpine draws as this route wanders' — used directly.
runs: lots of alpine draws as this route wanders

text:
You are at the right saddle when Concord is on one side of you and Lexington is on the other, and the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges rather than a steep crack system. If you are facing a crack system, you are at the Liberty Bell-Concord Notch and looking at the north face.

That is the notch test, and it is the one that matters, because the two saddles are a few hundred feet apart on the same ridge and both are reached from the same trailhead by the same path.

Arrival at this particular route, which is a different question from arrival at the notch: looking from the notch, start up the obvious crack in the middle of the wall. This route takes the centre of Concord's south face, climbs through a bulge, and continues trending left. Two right-facing corners put you at a tree right below the summit block.

So the count is: one crack in the middle, one bulge, two right-facing corners, one tree. If your line runs up the edge of the wall rather than its centre, you are on the tower's other south-face route.

Why the notch test and the route test both mention cracks without contradicting each other: at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch a steep crack system rises directly in front of you, which is the North Face. At the Concord-Lexington notch the wall reads as low-angle and gravelly overall, and this route's crack is the obvious feature up the middle of that easier-angled wall. Judge the wall first, then the line.

Descent: downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations.
runs: looking from the notch start up the obvious crack in the middle of the wall

text: Climbed by Fletch Taylor and Chris Dolejska on August 8, 1994 — the same day the pair also climbed Silver Star Mountain's northwest ridge, completing both routes within an 18-hour outing. Starting at the col between Vasiliki and Burgundy Spires with scrambling to a rightward-trending dihedral system below the south face, they instead stepped left onto fifth-class cracks: a single hand crack (5.7) leading to a finger crack (5.8+) and a belay. The second pitch climbs a 15-foot traverse left (5.9), then a widening finger crack (5.7) for about 50 feet to a large dihedral that leads to the summit. Described as a well-protected two- to three-pitch climb.
runs: at the col between vasiliki and burgundy spires with scrambling to a rightward trending dihedral system below the south face

text: Start in the steep, loose gully on the south side below the giant chockstone; look for a tree above a left-leaning crack. Lieback and stem the short 5.7 crack to belay at the tree, which carries old webbing.
runs: giant chockstone look for a tree above a left leaning

text: Above the second chockstone there is often an ice or rock step of up to about 8 ft - the technical crux of the route. A short screw is listed as optional; most parties find nuts or a slung tree instead.
runs: there is often an ice or rock step

text: Move out of the gully onto the South Spur, forced climbers' left onto the face for a short section in summer conditions, and follow the spur to the south summit. This is where the summer 800 ft version of the route finishes.
runs: forced climbers left onto the face for a

text:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
runs: short distance to the start of the winter commonwealth

text:
The cliffs are the marker, and the instruction is to overshoot them by 100 ft. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further left past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

What confirms it once you are in: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the first chockstone, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A second chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

The exit test for later: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn left before the gully ends — look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

And one descent warning that parties get wrong: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the middle summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.
runs: see the end of the gully it is possible to turn left before the
look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers left around the cliff

text: A moderate 4-5 pitch rock route up the steep (but not vertical) headwall visible just below the summit on the south side, topping out very near the true summit.
runs: just below the summit on the south side

text: Drop the steep, eroded boot path off the north side of the pass to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west to the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Climb the clearing and the loose scree above it to the enclosed cirque at about 8,700 ft, then take about five pitches, none harder than 5.7, up the centre of the headwall, topping out just southwest of the true summit.
runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir

text: Gain the upper South Rib and follow it back rightward. A chute leads onto a large ledge overlooking the west face, then a slab traverse leads toward the summit pyramid. Loose blocks sit on the ledges and rockfall is frequent, so keep the rope clear of them.
runs: onto a large ledge overlooking the west face

text: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir

text:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go west along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.
runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir

text:
The cirque is the arrival, and it is unmistakable even in cloud because it closes around you. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

Which clearing, which is the actual problem: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is east of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

Confirmation at the base: the technical pitches start up the centre of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

Preview it from Longs Pass. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.
runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir

text: Walk up the Sahale ski track toward Guye for about 3/4 to 1 mile; where it fades, climb the boulder field and slide alder to the base of the cliff. Traverse east along the base past Blood Sport to a taller talus fan, go up it to the rib, and climb about five pitches of low fifth-class rock, dirt and trees to the south summit. For the high point, traverse north over the middle summit, rappel into the gap, and scramble to the north summit.
runs: slide alder to the base of the cliff traverse east along the base

text: Begin at one of two obvious dihedrals on the west side of the ridge south of the peak (accessible from Blue Lake). The first pitch climbs either of two clean corners to the ridge crest with chickenheads and good face features (5.7). The memorable traverse pitch crosses the gapping cannon hole (5.8), a feature which appeared sometime in the 1980s or 1990s. The final pitch is low 5th class scrambling to the summit block.
runs: at one of two obvious dihedrals on the west side of the ridge
either of two clean corners to the ridge crest
a feature which appeared sometime in the 1980s or 1990s the final

text: From Darrington, drive SR-530 north about 8 miles to the Suiattle River Road (FS Road 26) and follow it east about 20 miles to the Downey Creek Trailhead, at about 1,450 ft. The trail starts just past the Downey Creek bridge on the north side of the road; parking is on the south side. The Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at a washout near milepost 4.5, leaving the trailhead reachable only on foot or by bike; check its status before going.
runs: just past the downey creek bridge on the

text: From a camp at Wing Lake, hike around the lake and up a moraine onto a permanent snowfield to an obvious col in the south ridge. A broad, loose gully on the west side of the ridge leads up toward the final summit blocks, where several class-3 lines can be pieced together to a small, airy summit block reached via a ~100-ft, highly exposed knife-edge. The route is normally done without a rope. Rock is loose in many places, so care must be taken to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below.
runs: onto a permanent snowfield to an obvious col in the south ridge a broad

text: Gained from Wing Lake by going around its north side, then up a moraine and permanent snowfield; a broad gully on the west side leads to the summit blocks.
runs: a broad gully on the west side leads to the

text: Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area/Lake Ann trailhead on SR 20 (milepost ~157.5, elev. ~4,850 ft; 40-car lot with privy). Follow the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (#740) about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass (the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann). Climb through meadows to Heather Pass (~2.6 mi, ~6,100 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus/boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake (~3.5-4 mi, ~5,700 ft; timbered campsites on the north side, water available) — this off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake (~5 mi, ~6,900 ft), the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake and reliable water into late summer. From Wing Lake, go around the right (north) side of the lake and aim for the obvious talus/snow gully leading into the couloir just south of the summit; climb this gully, then angle climber's-right out of it to avoid cliff bands directly below the col, topping out at the south col on the crest of the south ridge — the true start of the climbing.
runs: in the trees on the right as you

text:
Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area and Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 157.5 at about 4,850 ft, a 40-car lot with a privy. This is the Rainy Pass Lake Ann, not the Lake Ann below Mount Shuksan on the Mount Baker Highway; the two are about 80 km apart and share a name.

Follow the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail #740 about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass; the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann. Climb through meadows to Heather Pass at about 2.6 miles and 6,100 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus and boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake at about 3.5-4 miles and 5,700 ft, with timbered campsites on the north side and water. This off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake at about 5 miles and 6,900 ft, the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake.
runs: in the trees on the right as you

text: Pitch 1 climbs an obvious crack up the face to the 'U-notch' on the ridge; pitch 2 follows excellent cracks on the far side; pitches 3-4 are classic exposed knife-edge ridge ('B-Basin knife riding') ending in a short downclimb, after which the ridge broadens into mellow scrambling to the summit.
runs: climbs an obvious crack up the face to the u notch on the ridge

text: The ridge is gained from either its north or south side via moderate scrambling between South Twin's true summit and a subpeak about a quarter mile northeast. Climbers moving between North and South Twin cross the Sisters Glacier southbound to a bergschrund below the ridge, then climb up (favoring snow over rock where possible) to the ridge crest and follow it, mostly Class 3, with some low-5th variations, to the summit. Arrowtip Tower, on the lower part of the ridge, offers good rock climbing for parties looking for extra pitches.
runs: its north or south side via moderate scrambling between south

text: Park at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River (~1,200 ft) at the end of FR 38, reached via Mosquito Lake Road off WA-542. From the gate, most parties mountain-bike the old quarry/logging road system for roughly 6-7 miles and well over 2,000 ft of gain, threading several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie (GPS/GPX tracking is recommended here since wrong turns are common) before the road becomes too rough or overgrown to ride, usually marked by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes in the woods and pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot — brushy, wet, and occasionally overgrown but not hard to follow. The path drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and fades out at a red talus slope, which often holds snow well into summer. From the talus, traverse rightward (south) up and across, over a timbered rib, passing the ruins of an old miner's log cabin, then continue up into Orsino Creek Basin — the last reliable water source before the climb. From the basin, pick a line up onto the West Ridge; the standard start is an obvious notch in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft. Total foot travel from the bike cache to the summit is roughly 4 miles with substantial additional gain (combined bike + foot gain for the full approach runs about 6,100 ft), taking most parties 4-5 hours one-way. Watch for loose rock on the climbers' path and lower talus, and for lingering snow on the talus slope and approach gullies in early/mid-season, which can require an ice axe.
runs: the ruins of an old miner's log cabin

text:
Park at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River near 1,200 ft at the end of FR-38, reached via Mosquito Lake Road off WA-542. From the gate most parties mountain-bike the old quarry and logging road system for roughly 6-7 miles and well over 2,000 ft of gain, threading several forks near Dailey Prairie, until the road becomes too rough or overgrown to ride — usually marked by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. GPS or a GPX track is genuinely recommended on this network.

Stash bikes and pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot: brushy, wet, occasionally overgrown, but not hard to follow. It drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and fades out at a red talus slope which often holds snow well into summer.

From the talus, traverse rightward — south — up and across, over a timbered rib, past the ruins of an old miner's log cabin, then up into Orsino Creek Basin. Orsino Creek is the last reliable water before the climb.

About four miles of foot travel from the bike cache to the summit, four to five hours one way for most parties, with combined bike and foot gain around 6,100 ft.
runs: over a timbered rib past the ruins of an old miner's log cabin

text:
The ruins of an old log cabin are the one man-made thing on this approach and they are the checkpoint. From the red talus slope where the climbers' path fades, traverse right — south — up and across, cross a timbered rib, and pass the cabin ruins. If you have not passed a collapsed cabin, you have not made the traverse and you are still below the basin.

Orsino Creek is the last water and the entry to the basin. Fill up. There is nothing above it.

The base is an obvious notch in the ridge crest at about 5,200 ft, and you get to it up a steep loose dirt gully. That combination — an unpleasant slog up steep dirt, scree and talus, then a defined notch in a crest — is the arrival, and it works in cloud because a notch is a thing you stand in with air on the far side. This is the standard start and it is where the West Ridge is gained down low.

The discriminator against the other route out of this basin, and it is a single number: the North Ridge route continues higher and further climber's left — north — up basin snow or talus to a saddle around 5,800 ft between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge. So 5,200 ft and the obvious notch is the West Ridge; 5,800 ft and a saddle between two peaks is the North Ridge. Six hundred feet and a bearing separate two routes that share every step of the approach up to the basin.

The rock confirms the range: dunite, olivine-rich, exceptionally grippy, like coarse sandpaper. It is why parties choose to gain the ridge low rather than high — to maximise time on it.

Higher up, the false-summit bypass is worth carrying before you need it: leave the crest to the right — south — traverse ledges, and regain the crest about 200 yards short of the false summit, roughly 500 ft above where you left it. Staying exactly on the crest through that step is what forces parties into an improvised rappel.
runs: an obvious notch in the ridge crest at about
an unpleasant slog up steep dirt scree and talus

text: From SR 20 at milepost 82 near Concrete, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive about 24 miles to FS Road 1152, directly across from Shannon Creek Campground. Turn left on 1152, then take a sharp right onto spur 1152-014 and follow it to the road end at about 2,500 ft. The gravel can be potholed but is passable to most cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass is required to park.
runs: 24 miles to fs road 1152 directly across from

text: Named after the Neil Young song, Southern Man splits off from the Direct East Buttress about halfway up and climbs the south-facing headwall on SEWS's upper south side to the summit. First ascended by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Leaghan Falley, August 2008 (aided at 5.9+ C1); freed by B. Matthews and Bryan Burdo in 2010 at 5.11d (a September 2009 ascent by Burdo at 5.12a is unconfirmed).
runs: about halfway up and climbs the south facing headwall on

text: Hike up the cairned Spire Gully to the last large tree, traverse right across talus (snow early season) to the gully that leads to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress before reaching the notch. Climb the shared Direct East Buttress pitches, break out left about halfway up onto the south-facing headwall, and follow its crack pitches to the summit.
runs: to the gully that leads to the notch between
then traverse left to the base of the

text: Same as Direct East Buttress: park at the hairpin pullout on Highway 20, hike Spire Gully (cairned) to the last large tree, traverse right across talus/snow to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress. Southern Man shares the East Buttress's first pitches, then splits off around halfway up to climb the south-facing headwall on the upper south side of the peak for its final 5 pitches (9 total) to the top.
runs: then traverse left to the base of the
the south facing headwall on the upper south side

text:
Same as the Direct East Buttress: park at the hairpin pullout on Highway 20 east of Washington Pass. This is the east-side trailhead, not the Blue Lake trailhead used by the spire's west-side routes.

Nine pitches. The route shares the East Buttress's first pitches, then splits off around halfway up to climb the south-facing headwall on the upper south side of the peak for its final five pitches.
runs: the south facing headwall on the upper south side

text:
Hike spire gully, which is cairned, to the last large tree. That tree is the turn. From it, traverse right across talus and snow to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress.

So the sequence is three moves and a tree: up the cairned gully to the last large tree, right across talus, then left to the buttress base. The tree is the only thing in that sequence you can put a hand on, which is why it is the marker rather than the gully.

Why the notch matters even though you do not go to it: the gully you aim at is the one running to the gap between the two spires, the same continuous cleft that on the west side is the chockstone-filled chimney. It is the biggest feature on this side of the group. Aim at it, then step left before reaching it.

So the negative test is: if you have reached the notch itself you have gone up too far, and if you are on the far side of the cleft you are on North Early Winters Spire, where Flycatcher Buttress starts from a flat ledge.

What separates this route from the east buttress it shares a start with, and it is a decision made halfway up rather than at the base: Southern Man splits off around mid-height onto the south-facing headwall. Its own belays are described as vague and not yet fixed, which is itself a tell: do not expect a fully bolted rap line if you need to bail from the upper headwall. Natural anchors would be required there.

Descent: from the summit, the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed fifth-class section to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.
runs: then traverse left to the base of the

text: Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at about road mile 20, elevation roughly 2,100 ft, and park in the trailhead lot. The climb starts by leaving the parking area and backtracking a short way downstream to find a log or a ford across the Cascade River, then picking up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek. This is the same start the East Ridge uses; the trailhead-to-glacier approach is identical for both.
runs: path on the west side of eldorado creek

text: Continue across the McAllister to the Marble Creek-McAllister pass, the lowest gap on the southwest side of the glacier, and cross onto the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.
runs: the lowest gap on the southwest side of the glacier

text: The hike-in to the Southwest Buttress follows the identical trailhead-to-glacier approach as the East Ridge: from the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River/Eldorado Creek near the parking area (backtrack downstream to find a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest (no water on this stretch) to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback up past 6,000 ft, and drop via a short Class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water, a good lower camp/bail-out point). From the basin, ascend 20-30-degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier at about 7,500 ft - rope up for crevasse hazard from here on - and establish a high camp on rock/moraine near the glacier shoulder for the multi-day stay. Where the Southwest Buttress approach diverges is the final glacier traverse: from camp, continue across the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister Glacier, heading toward the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The base of the Southwest Buttress is reached via a prominent gully - often snow-filled year-round - that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
runs: path on the west side of eldorado creek
a prominent gully often snow filled year round

text:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
runs: path on the west side of eldorado creek
a prominent gully often snow filled year round

text:
The base is the toe of the buttress at the foot of a prominent, often year-round snow gully, and the gully is located by descending — it starts about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

At the top of that gully there is a fork, and it is the one thing on this peak most worth getting right. This route goes around to the right. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes straight up from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

The strongest negative test is published as a warning and it is worth carrying verbatim: do not climb directly below the ridge crest at the start. That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 overhanging terrain on loose rock. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

Confirm on pitch one: it is a full rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly right, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

And confirm by which col you crossed: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.
runs: about 700 vertical feet below the marble creek mcallister pass

text: From I-90 Exit 52 (Snoqualmie Pass West), turn north under the freeway onto Alpental Road and follow it about 1.3 miles to the road end at the Alpental ski area lot, the Snow Lake trailhead, at about 3,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is required.
runs: a northwest forest pass is required to park

text: From the summit, several parties instead scramble roughly 30 feet north along the summit ridge, descend a short gully/chimney, follow easy slabs down and north to a major gully, work up to a narrow notch in the summit ridge, cross it (a belay is prudent), and continue north to a descent gully leading down the north end of the west face — but for most parties the simplest option is to rappel the South Face's equipped stations (about four rappels) back to Pineapple Pass and retrace the approach; rappelling the loose east-side gully carries notable rockfall hazard and is not recommended.
runs: follow easy slabs down and north to a major gully work
a narrow notch in the summit ridge cross

text: From I-90 Exit 52, turn northwest onto Alpental Road and follow it to the Alpental ski area parking lot (Snow Lake Trailhead).
runs: turn northwest onto alpental road and follow it to the alpental

text: From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, follow the Snow Lake trail about a mile and a half, fork toward Source Lake, cross the talus and start up toward Pineapple Pass on the standard line. The difference is at the top. Do not finish the gully to the pass. Break off to the north of it and climb the open books on the face above instead. This is the route parties take when the South Face is backed up, and it is deliberately the path of least resistance between The Tooth Fairy and the South Face. About 4.8 km and 2,500 ft from the car.
runs: the path of least resistance between the tooth fairy and the south face

text:
The arrival test is a thing you do not do: do not go up to Pineapple Pass. Hike the stable talus toward the pass and then leave it, heading north of the gully that finishes at the pass. If you have stood in the notch at Pineapple Pass, you have overshot the start of this route and you are at the start of the South Face.

What you are looking for on the rock: open books. Pitches one and two climb open-book corners that begin north of the Pineapple Pass gully, and they lead to a left-facing slab. Corner, corner, then slab facing left. That sequence is the confirmation, and none of it requires seeing the summit.

And a third-pitch check if you are still unsure: pitch three finds three cracks running up to an overhang, and the route face-climbs to the left of those three cracks. Three cracks under a roof, and you go left of them. If you are climbing the cracks themselves you have drifted right.

How it differs from its two neighbours: The Tooth Fairy is further left again and goes at 5.9; the South Face starts from the notch at the top of the pass at 5.4. This route sits between them, both physically and in difficulty, at 5.5. If your first pitch feels like 5.9, you have gone too far left.

A warning that belongs with the finding: this face is loose, and it sits above the popular routes. Being on the correct start also means being above other people.
runs: that begin north of the pineapple pass gully

text: A full-value, remote adventure alpine rock climb that is infrequently traveled and requires real route-finding rather than following an obvious line. Roughly 19 ropelengths (60m) wind up the rib and around towers: intermittent treed/sandy ledges, slabs, and short steep steps lead up an indistinct crest for about 500 vertical feet until it becomes a defined, knife-edged ridge (marked by a large open slab visible on climber's left from a distance); the rib then relaxes into low-angled, sometimes loose/sandy corners for another ~400 feet; the upper climb is steeper and more continuously exposed, featuring prominent gendarmes, a sharp ridge traverse, a left-trending ramp below a steep white headwall, and a final summit block on Crystal Lake Tower, then a notch and ridge crest that lead on to the westernmost Chessman.
runs: ledges slabs and short steep steps lead up

text: Indistinct crest; intermittent treed, sandy ledges, slabs, and short steep steps.
runs: intermittent treed sandy ledges slabs and short steep steps

text: Rib becomes less distinct again; low-angled corners, some filled with loose blocks and sand.
runs: low angled corners some filled with loose blocks and sand

text: From Cle Elum, take SR-970 east 7 miles to US-97, turn north on US-97 over Blewett Pass, and at milepost 178 turn left onto Ingalls Creek Road. Cross Peshastin Creek, bear left, and follow the road to its end at the trailhead. From Leavenworth, go east on US-2 for 4 miles, turn right onto US-97 south and go 7 miles to the same turn.
runs: at milepost 178 turn left onto ingalls creek road cross peshastin creek bear left

text: Elevation sources disagree slightly: Fred Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide describes Crystal Lake Tower as a pinnacle at about 7,800 ft just below McClellan Peak's summit ridge, while Mountain Project lists 7,923 ft for the same coordinates used in our database (47.46872, -120.79532) — likely a DEM-derived figure for that exact point. Beckey's guide also notes the route's practical high point continues past the tower's cairned summit to a separate, slightly higher rounded point on the ridge (~8,000 ft) — climbers should be aware the first cairn is not the true top. No specific rappel count/anchor sequence for descending the SW Rib itself was found in available sources; only the general Fantasia Saddle/Fantasia Pond descent option is documented.
runs: crystal lake tower as a pinnacle at about

text: A pair of pyramidal twin summits in the Entiat Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) land in Chelan County. The sharper south summit (8,392 ft) is the true high point; the north butte (8,080 ft) sits about a half-mile away across a connecting basin. The name comes from their twin-lensed profile as seen from the Entiat River valley. First ascent of the south peak was made August 20, 1953 by Rowland Tabor and Dwight Crowder. This route follows the southwest ridge/west-facing slopes — the standard line on South Spectacle Butte — reached via a long, mostly cross-country approach through Leroy Basin and the Ice Lakes basin. Traffic is light; most parties combine it with Ice Lakes camping or a Leroy-Carne loop.
runs: first ascent of the south peak was made

text: Established in August 2006 by Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton after a grueling approach, this route starts in the center of Spectre's south face and climbs about 800 feet of runout terrain into a 'deep, spooky' chimney that is completely enclosed inside the mountain at times, then continues on exposed face climbing past an offwidth section before a ridge traverse gains the summit. The route is noted for being largely devoid of crack protection through its runout sections.
runs: starts in the center of spectre's south face

text: As with the south ridge route, access is via the Hannegan Pass Trailhead and Easy Ridge, crossing a col to the right of Mount Challenger's summit before descending several miles to a camp below Phantom Peak's south face, from which the south face of Spectre is reached.
runs: to a camp below phantom peak's south face

text: Spectre Peak (7,952'; a LIDAR-based figure gives 7,953') sits on the western slope of the Northern Pickets — it's grouped thematically with neighboring Ghost Peak and Phantom Peak near Swiss Peak and Mount Challenger, part of the Northern Pickets traverse line (Luna-Fury-Swiss-Spectre-Phantom-Crooked Thumb-Ghost-Challenger). It is one of the most remote and rarely climbed summits in the Pickets, with only two documented technical routes on record: Haunted Wall (IV 5.9+, 2,100', Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton, Aug 2006) and this South Ridge line.
runs: on the western slope of the northern pickets

text: From the river, switchback steeply back up onto Easy Ridge and then follow the crest itself. This is a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge with almost no shade; flowing water shows up relatively early along it, but the first-ascent party warned this stretch would be brutal later in the season and in dry years, so fill up while you can. Continue along and over Easy Peak to the established bivy beyond it, roughly a ten-hour day with a full pack from the trailhead.
runs: brutal later in the season and in dry years

text: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32). From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. From the pass, stay on the maintained trail as it drops past Boundary Camp and Copper Creek Camp into the Chilliwack valley; roughly two miles beyond Copper Creek an easily missed side path leads down to the Chilliwack River ford (about 2,750 ft), and the Easy Ridge path climbs steeply from the far bank. From here it is sustained, largely cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned it becomes brutal later in the season and in dry years. Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.
runs: brutal later in the season and in dry years

text: Starts with two pitches on the slabby face just left of a small, deteriorating pocket glacier under the large gully on the east face. Above the slab, the face forces you left over a small rock wall, then continues straight up for a couple more pitches through brush and small trees. The route then narrows and traverses right on a narrow, jungle-filled ledge with significant exposure down the main gully; after about 50 ft, when clean rock appears above, head straight up it and belay as soon as possible to avoid rope drag (or belay on the ledge itself). Another half pitch gains the upper SE ridge, from which you scramble around to the right to reach the top. The first-ascent party took 7-8 hours on the route and arrived at the summit after dark, bivying there.
runs: pitches on the slabby face just left of
deteriorating pocket glacier under the large gully on the east face

belay as soon as possible to avoid rope drag or belay on the ledge

text: Start up the obvious slabby rock face just left of the small pocket glacier under the main east-face gully.
